abstract.text:
Can any secrets still be shed by that much studied, uniquely integrable,
Elliptic Billiard? Starting by examining the family of 3-periodic trajectories and
the loci of their Triangular Centers, one obtains a beautiful and variegated gallery
of curves: ellipses, quartics, sextics, circles, and even a stationary point. Secondly,
one notices this family conserves an intriguing ratio: Inradius-to-Circumradius. In
turn this implies three conservation corollaries: (i) the sum of bounce angle cosines,
(ii) the product of excentral cosines, and (iii) the ratio of excentral-to-orbit areas.
Monge’s Orthoptic Circle’s close relation to 4-periodic Billiard trajectories is well-
known. Its geometry provided clues with which to generalize 3-periodic invariants
to trajectories of an arbitrary number of edges. This was quite unexpected. Indeed,
the Elliptic Billiard did surprise us!

objects.caption: Fig. 3: Notable Triangle Points, referred to as X i, after Kimberling [15]. Left: The Incenter X 1 is the intersection of angular bisectors, and center of the Incircle (green), a circle tangent to the sides at three Intouchpoints (green dots), its radius is the Inradius r. The Barycenter X 2 is where lines drawn from the vertices to opposite sides’ midpoints meet. Side midpoints define the Medial Triangle (red). The Circumcenter X 3 is the intersection of perpendicular bisectors, the center of the Circumcircle (purple) whose radius is the Circumradius R. The Orthocenter X 4 is where altitudes concur. Their feet define the Orthic Triangle (orange). X 5 is the center of the 9-Point (or Euler) Circle (pink): it passes through each side’s midpoint, altitude feet, and Euler Points [32]. The Feuerbach Point X 11 is the single point of contact between the Incircle and the 9-Point Circle. Right: given a reference triangle P 1 P 2 P 3 (blue), the Excenters P 1 0 P 2 0 P 3 0 are pairwise intersections of lines through the P i and perpendicular to the bisectors. This triad defines the Excentral Triangle (green). The Excircles (dashed green) are centered on the Excenters and are tangent to the triangle sides at the Extouch Points e i, i = 1, 2, 3. Lines drawn from each Excenter through sides’ midpoints (dashed red) concur at the Mittenpunkt X 9. Also shown is Feuerbach’s Theorem [32]: besides the Incircle, the 9-Pt Circle (pink) touches each Excircle at a single point (pink dots), the vertices of the Feuerbach Triangle.

objects.caption: Fig. 5: Gaspard Monge (1746–1818) discovered that the locus of points whose tangents to a given ellipse subtend a right angle is a circle (red), called the Orthoptic Circle. Its connection with Billiards is remarkable [5]: From a point P 1 0 on the circle, shoot two rays tangent to the ellipse, intersecting them with the circle at P 2 0 and P 4 0. From either one shoot one new tangent ray and obtain P 3 0. Four surprises: (i) the intersections form a rectangle (green); (ii) the points of tangency with the ellipse define a parallelogram (blue), which is (iii) a billiard orbit of the ellipse; (iv) all N = 4 non-intersecting orbits are constant perimeter parallelograms. supercut.text: The Elliptic Billiard (EB) consists of a particle moving with constant velocity in the interior of an ellipse, bouncing elastically against its boundary.
The paper asks whether this exhaustively studied integrable system still has surprises.
In 2011, we uploaded a video [19, pl#2] showing the family of 3-periodic trajectories as a continuous set of rotating triangles.
Over the next few years there surfaced elegant proofs showing that the locus of the Incenter [8, 23], Barycenter [9, 25], Circumcenter [7, 9], and Orthocenter [9] were all ellipses.
This motivated an exploratory survey of loci of many triangle centers.
Beyond loci, the N = 3 family revealed an amazing property: the ratio of Inradius to Circumradius is invariant.
At this point a remarkable object steps in, coaxing us into a breakthrough: Monge’s Orthoptic Circle, Figure 5.
The orthoptic circle links the 3-periodic family to 4-periodic orbits and suggests how to generalize invariants to arbitrary N.
Its connection with Billiards is remarkable [5]: From a point P 1 0 on the circle, shoot two rays tangent to the ellipse, intersecting them with the circle at P 2 0 and P 4 0.

admission.original:
Can any secrets still be shed by that much studied, uniquely integrable,
Elliptic Billiard? Starting by examining the family of 3-periodic trajectories and
the loci of their Triangular Centers, one obtains a beautiful and variegated gallery
of curves: ellipses, quartics, sextics, circles, and even a stationary point. Secondly,
one notices this family conserves an intriguing ratio: Inradius-to-Circumradius. In
turn this implies three conservation corollaries: (i) the sum of bounce angle cosines,
(ii) the product of excentral cosines, and (iii) the ratio of excentral-to-orbit areas.
Monge’s Orthoptic Circle’s close relation to 4-periodic Billiard trajectories is well-
known. Its geometry provided clues with which to generalize 3-periodic invariants
to trajectories of an arbitrary number of edges. This was quite unexpected. Indeed,
the Elliptic Billiard did surprise us!

Left: The Incenter X 1 is the intersection of angular bisectors, and center of the Incircle (green), a circle tangent to the sides at three Intouchpoints (green dots), its radius is the Inradius r. The Barycenter X 2 is where lines drawn from the vertices to opposite sides’ midpoints meet. Side midpoints define the Medial Triangle (red). The Circumcenter X 3 is the intersection of perpendicular bisectors, the center of the Circumcircle (purple) whose radius is the Circumradius R. The Orthocenter X 4 is where altitudes concur. The Feuerbach Point X 11 is the single point of contact between the Incircle and the 9-Point Circle. Lines drawn from each Excenter through sides’ midpoints (dashed red) concur at the Mittenpunkt X 9. Also shown is Feuerbach’s Theorem [32]: besides the Incircle, the 9-Pt Circle (pink) touches each Excircle at a single point (pink dots), the vertices of the Feuerbach Triangle.

admission.original: Fig. 5: Gaspard Monge (1746–1818) discovered that the locus of points whose tangents to a given ellipse subtend a right angle is a circle (red), called the Orthoptic Circle. Its connection with Billiards is remarkable [5]: From a point P 1 0 on the circle, shoot two rays tangent to the ellipse, intersecting them with the circle at P 2 0 and P 4 0. From either one shoot one new tangent ray and obtain P 3 0. abstract.text:
Can any secrets still be shed by that much studied, uniquely integrable,
Elliptic Billiard? Starting by examining the family of 3-periodic trajectories and
the loci of their Triangular Centers, one obtains a beautiful and variegated gallery
of curves: ellipses, quartics, sextics, circles, and even a stationary point. Secondly,
one notices this family conserves an intriguing ratio: Inradius-to-Circumradius. In
turn this implies three conservation corollaries: (i) the sum of bounce angle cosines,
(ii) the product of excentral cosines, and (iii) the ratio of excentral-to-orbit areas.
Monge’s Orthoptic Circle’s close relation to 4-periodic Billiard trajectories is well-
known. Its geometry provided clues with which to generalize 3-periodic invariants
to trajectories of an arbitrary number of edges. This was quite unexpected. Indeed,
the Elliptic Billiard did surprise us!

objects.caption: Fig. 1: Particle trajectories in an Elliptic Billiard. Top left: the first four segments of a trajectory starting at P 1 along the red arrow, bouncing elastically at P 2 (reflecting about normals n̂ i), etc. Top right: a 3-periodic trajectory. Bottom: quasi-periodic regimes tangent to an elliptic (left) or hyperbolic (right) Caustic. The first (resp. second) regime is established if a segment passes outside (resp. between) the foci (black dots). Video [19, pl#1]
objects.label: Figure 1
objects.plain_language: Particle trajectories in an elliptic billiard, showing ordinary reflection, a 3-periodic orbit, and quasi-periodic regimes tangent to elliptic or hyperbolic caustics.
objects.why_it_matters: Introduces the basic billiard dynamics and the two caustic regimes used throughout the paper.

objects.caption: Fig. 2: An N = 3 orbit (blue), its Incircle (transparent green), Incenter (green dot) and Intouch Points (brown dots). Over the N = 3 family, the Incenter locus is a perfect ellipse (green), while the Intouchpoints produce a self-intersecting sextic (dashed brown). Video [19, pl#2]
objects.label: Figure 2
objects.plain_language: A 3-periodic orbit with its incircle and incenter; over the family, the incenter traces an ellipse while the intouch points trace a self-intersecting sextic.
objects.why_it_matters: Shows the contrast between a simple elliptic locus and a complicated sextic locus.

objects.caption: Fig. 3: Notable Triangle Points, referred to as X i, after Kimberling [15]. Left: The Incenter X 1 is the intersection of angular bisectors, and center of the Incircle (green), a circle tangent to the sides at three Intouchpoints (green dots), its radius is the Inradius r. The Barycenter X 2 is where lines drawn from the vertices to opposite sides’ midpoints meet. Side midpoints define the Medial Triangle (red). The Circumcenter X 3 is the intersection of perpendicular bisectors, the center of the Circumcircle (purple) whose radius is the Circumradius R. The Orthocenter X 4 is where altitudes concur. Their feet define the Orthic Triangle (orange). X 5 is the center of the 9-Point (or Euler) Circle (pink): it passes through each side’s midpoint, altitude feet, and Euler Points [32]. The Feuerbach Point X 11 is the single point of contact between the Incircle and the 9-Point Circle. Right: given a reference triangle P 1 P 2 P 3 (blue), the Excenters P 1 0 P 2 0 P 3 0 are pairwise intersections of lines through the P i and perpendicular to the bisectors. This triad defines the Excentral Triangle (green). The Excircles (dashed green) are centered on the Excenters and are tangent to the triangle sides at the Extouch Points e i, i = 1, 2, 3. Lines drawn from each Excenter through sides’ midpoints (dashed red) concur at the Mittenpunkt X 9. Also shown is Feuerbach’s Theorem [32]: besides the Incircle, the 9-Pt Circle (pink) touches each Excircle at a single point (pink dots), the vertices of the Feuerbach Triangle.
objects.label: Figure 3
objects.plain_language: Reference diagram of notable triangle points and derived triangles: incenter, barycenter, circumcenter, orthocenter, 9-point center, Feuerbach point, excenters, excentral triangle, and Mittenpunkt.
objects.why_it_matters: Provides the geometrical vocabulary used to describe loci and invariants.

objects.caption: Fig. 4: Poncelet’s Porism states that given two nested ellipses, if one closed trajectory with N sides can be found starting at a point P on the boundary of the outer while remaining tangent to the inner, then every boundary point (e.g., P 0) can initiate an N -trajectory, i.e., there exists a one-dimensional family of closed trajectories.
objects.label: Figure 4
objects.plain_language: Illustration of Poncelet's porism for two nested ellipses, showing that one closed trajectory implies a one-parameter family.
objects.why_it_matters: Frames the elliptic billiard as a Poncelet porism, a key integrability fact.

objects.caption: Fig. 5: Gaspard Monge (1746–1818) discovered that the locus of points whose tangents to a given ellipse subtend a right angle is a circle (red), called the Orthoptic Circle. Its connection with Billiards is remarkable [5]: From a point P 1 0 on the circle, shoot two rays tangent to the ellipse, intersecting them with the circle at P 2 0 and P 4 0. From either one shoot one new tangent ray and obtain P 3 0. Four surprises: (i) the intersections form a rectangle (green); (ii) the points of tangency with the ellipse define a parallelogram (blue), which is (iii) a billiard orbit of the ellipse; (iv) all N = 4 non-intersecting orbits are constant perimeter parallelograms. Video [19, pl#5]
objects.label: Figure 5
objects.plain_language: Monge's orthoptic circle for an ellipse and its connection to 4-periodic billiard orbits, which are constant-perimeter parallelograms.
objects.why_it_matters: The orthoptic circle is the clue used to generalize 3-periodic invariants to N > 3.

objects.caption: Fig. 6: Triangular Orbits in an EB and their Incenter. Video [19, pl#6]
objects.label: Figure 6
objects.plain_language: Triangular billiard orbits in an elliptic billiard and their incenters; subfigures show one orbit with bisectors and three orbits with their incenters and confocal caustic.
objects.why_it_matters: Illustrates the basic N=3 geometry used for the incenter locus discussion.

objects.caption: Fig. 7: Loci of major triangle centers are ellipses.
objects.label: Figure 7
objects.plain_language: Loci of X1, X2, X3, X4, and X5 over the 3-periodic family, all ellipses.
objects.why_it_matters: Summarizes the elliptic-locus phenomenon for major triangle centers.

objects.caption: Fig. 8: An EB (black) is shown with its axes rotated (to save space), as well as an N = 3 orbit (blue) and its Excentral Triangle (solid green). The locus of Excenters (vertices of the Excentral Triangle) is an ellipse similar to a perpendicular copy of the locus of the Incenter (shown solid green inside the EB). Video [19, pl#8]
objects.label: Figure 8
objects.plain_language: An elliptic billiard with a 3-periodic orbit and its excentral triangle; the excenter locus is an ellipse related to the incenter locus.
objects.why_it_matters: Shows that the excentral triangle is an exceptional derived triangle with an elliptic locus.

objects.caption: Fig. 9: The vertices of the Intouch (green), Feuerbach (blue), and Medial (red) Triangles produce non-elliptic loci. Surprisingly, the Extouchpoints as well as the Feuerbach Point X 11 (both shown brown), are identical to the N = 3 Caustic. Video [19, pl#9]
objects.label: Figure 9
objects.plain_language: Loci of vertices of intouch, Feuerbach, and medial triangles are non-elliptic, while extouchpoints and the Feuerbach point coincide with the caustic.
objects.why_it_matters: Contrasts non-elliptic derived-triangle loci with the special extouch and Feuerbach loci.

objects.caption: Fig. 10: The EB (black), as well as an N = 3 orbit (blue), with P 1 the starting vertex, and the Caustic (brown). Also shown are the orbit’s Incircle (green) and 9-Point Circle (pink), whose single point of contact is the Feuerbach Point X 11. Shown also is its anticomplement X 100, and the three Extouchpoints e 1, e 2, e 3. Remarkable properties include: X 11 and the Extouchpoints sweep the Caustic, and X 100 sweeps the Billiard (in opposite directions). Video [19, pl#12]
objects.label: Figure 10
objects.plain_language: A 3-periodic orbit with incircle, 9-point circle, Feuerbach point, its anticomplement, and extouchpoints; X11 and extouchpoints sweep the caustic while X100 sweeps the billiard.
objects.why_it_matters: Illustrates the Feuerbach-point and anticomplement locus dichotomy.

objects.caption: Fig. 11: Affine proof (pun intended!) [24] for the Stationarity of the Mittenpunkt. Left: N = 3 orbit (blue), its Excentral Triangle (green), and the construction for X 9, the Mittenpunkt, stationary at the center of the Billiard (black). Right: Under a suitable affine transform, the Billiard becomes a circle, side midpoints become chord midpoints (distance ratios are preserved). By symmetry, lines connecting transformed Excenters to the latter must concur at the circle center, uniquely identified under the transform with the Billiard center. Video [19, pl#13]
objects.label: Figure 11
objects.plain_language: Affine-transformation proof that the Mittenpunkt X9 is stationary at the billiard center.
objects.why_it_matters: Gives the geometric reason for the stationary Mittenpunkt and motivates the N > 3 generalization.

objects.caption: Fig. 12: A 3-periodic (blue), a starting vertex P 1, the Incircle (green), Circumcircle (purple), and 9-Point Circle (pink), whose centers are X 1, X 3, and X 5, and radii are the inradius r, circumradius R, and 9-Point Circle radius r 9.
objects.label: Figure 12
objects.plain_language: A 3-periodic orbit with its incircle, circumcircle, and 9-point circle, showing centers X1, X3, X5 and radii r, R, r9.
objects.why_it_matters: Defines the radii whose ratios become conserved quantities.

objects.caption: Fig. 13: Left: the EB (black), an N = 3 orbit (blue), and its Excentral Triangle (green). Middle: both the orbit and its Excentral are shown in an “elementary” configuration: two vertices are pinned to the x axis and a third one is set free, in such a way that triangles here are similar to their counterparts on the left. Isocurves of constant cosine sum are shown in terms of the position of the free vertex. Notice only the orbit triangle follows such an isocurve (dashed blue). Right: Here isocurves of cosine product are shown, showing the free vertex of the Excentral Triangle moves along one (dashed green). Video [19, pl#15]
objects.label: Figure 13
objects.plain_language: Visualization of constant cosine-sum and cosine-product isocurves for the orbit and its excentral triangle.
objects.why_it_matters: Provides geometric intuition for the conservation of cosine sum and product.

objects.caption: Fig. 14: Left: Circular Locus of Q 1 (or Q 2). Right: The Excentral Triangle’s six intersections with its reflection about its Symmedian Point (congruent with X 9) is a circle. Video 1, Video 2 [19, pl#16,17]
objects.label: Figure 14
objects.plain_language: A circular locus for points Q1/Q2 and a circle formed by intersections of the excentral triangle with its reflection about its symmedian point.
objects.why_it_matters: Introduces the circular locus that later generalizes to N > 4.

objects.caption: Fig. 15: Left: N = 4 (resp. Right: N = 5) orbits shown in blue. The dashed red lines connect vertices of the Tangential (green) to orbit sides’ midpoints. Notice they intersect at the center of the Billiard, a type of generalized Mittenpunkt. Also shown are (dashed green) perpendiculars dropped from Tangential Vertices onto orbit sides. Their feet lie on and sweep the Caustic (brown). Video 1, Video 2 [19, pl#18,19].
objects.label: Figure 15
objects.plain_language: Generalized Mittenpunkt construction for N=4 and N=5 orbits: lines from tangential-polygon vertices to side midpoints concur at the billiard center, and perpendicular feet sweep the caustic.
objects.why_it_matters: Shows the N > 3 analogues of the Mittenpunkt and extouchpoint properties.

objects.caption: Fig. 16: The construction of a circular locus for N = 5, 6. Video 1, Video 2 [19, pl#20,21]
objects.label: Figure 16
objects.plain_language: Construction of a circular locus for N=5 and N=6 using intersections of a tangential edge with the reflection of the next tangential edge.
objects.why_it_matters: Illustrates the generalized circular-locus theorem for N > 4.

objects.plain_language: Joachimsthal invariant at bounces: half the dot product of the incoming unit velocity with the gradient of the ellipse boundary is a positive constant for all bounces.
objects.why_it_matters: This invariant gamma controls the constant perimeter and many later conservation laws.

objects.plain_language: Gradient of the ellipse boundary at the i-th bounce point (x_i, y_i).
objects.why_it_matters: Used in the definition of gamma and in the proof of the circular locus.

objects.plain_language: The conserved inradius-to-circumradius ratio equals gamma times perimeter minus four.
objects.why_it_matters: Central conservation law from which cosine-sum, cosine-product, and area-ratio corollaries follow.

objects.plain_language: Triangle identity: the sum of the three internal angle cosines equals one plus r/R.
objects.why_it_matters: Since r/R is constant, this implies conservation of the sum of cosines.

objects.plain_language: Product of absolute excentral-angle cosines equals r/(4R).
objects.why_it_matters: Since r/R is constant, the product of excentral cosines is conserved.

objects.plain_language: Area ratio of a triangle to its orthic triangle equals twice the orthic circumradius over the orthic inradius.
objects.why_it_matters: Used to prove conservation of the excentral-to-orbit area ratio.

objects.plain_language: Radius of the circular locus r* can be expressed as L divided by (r/R + 4), equivalently 1/gamma.
objects.why_it_matters: Identifies the circular locus radius with the inverse of the Joachimsthal invariant.

objects.plain_language: Expression for the constant perimeter L in terms of gamma and the squared gradient norms at the bounces.
objects.why_it_matters: Provides a route to compute L from the orbit geometry and generalizes to any N.

objects.plain_language: Momentum conservation condition between consecutive bounces: the unit velocity is orthogonal to the sum of consecutive gradients.
objects.why_it_matters: Key step in the proof that the generalized circular locus has radius 1/gamma.

supercut.text: The Elliptic Billiard (EB) consists of a particle moving with constant velocity in the interior of an ellipse, bouncing elastically against its boundary.
The paper asks whether this exhaustively studied integrable system still has surprises.
In 2011, we uploaded a video [19, pl#2] showing the family of 3-periodic trajectories as a continuous set of rotating triangles.
Over the next few years there surfaced elegant proofs showing that the locus of the Incenter [8, 23], Barycenter [9, 25], Circumcenter [7, 9], and Orthocenter [9] were all ellipses.
This motivated an exploratory survey of loci of many triangle centers.
Beyond loci, the N = 3 family revealed an amazing property: the ratio of Inradius to Circumradius is invariant.
At this point a remarkable object steps in, coaxing us into a breakthrough: Monge’s Orthoptic Circle, Figure 5.
The orthoptic circle links the 3-periodic family to 4-periodic orbits and suggests how to generalize invariants to arbitrary N.
Its connection with Billiards is remarkable [5]: From a point P 1 0 on the circle, shoot two rays tangent to the ellipse, intersecting them with the circle at P 2 0 and P 4 0.
